subject: history_social
passage: At Mamallapuram, on the coast of Tamil Nadu in southern India, the Pallava kings of the seventh and eighth centuries had temples and sculptures carved directly out of granite outcrops. Many of the monuments were never completed: carvings stop partway, and some surfaces show only rough outlines. Archaeologist Kavitha Sundaram hypothesizes that the monuments were carved at the same time by many crews working at once, rather than one after another over many decades.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sundaram's hypothesis?

choices.A: Stone chips and worn tools discarded during carving lie in one thick layer across the site rather than in separate layers.
choices.B: Several of the completed monuments at the site were later used as landmarks by sailors approaching the coast from the east.
choices.C: The granite at Mamallapuram is extremely hard, so carving even a small shrine would have required many months of work.
choices.D: The style of the carving changes noticeably from one monument to the next, in a sequence that matches changes in Pallava sculpture over a century.

explanation.why: Sundaram's hypothesis is about timing: many crews at once, not one project after another. Debris from carving is a good test, because work done at the same time leaves one layer while work spread over decades leaves layers. A sequence of changing styles would instead suggest work spread out over time.
explanation.A: Correct. A single layer of carving debris across the whole site is what many crews working at once would leave, while work spread over decades would leave layered deposits.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The later use of the monuments has nothing to do with how the carving was organized.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How long each shrine took does not show whether the crews worked at the same time or in sequence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A sequence of styles spanning a century suggests that the monuments were carved one after another, which goes against the hypothesis.
